---
title: "A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation"
---

## Start with a physiological problem

A small aquatic animal and a mammal must both deliver oxygen to living cells.
They face the same physical need but differ in body size, body organisation,
environment and activity. Explaining their differences requires more than
listing organs. We need to connect a structure to a process, identify the
constraint that the structure addresses, and ask what evidence supports the
explanation.

After this unit, you should be able to connect cells, tissues and organ systems;
explain an exchange constraint using size and distance; recognise the four
primary tissue categories from described features; construct a negative-feedback
explanation; and distinguish an individual's response from evolutionary change.
Use the [slides](lec.qmd), then the [exercises](exercise.qmd) and
[self-check quiz](quiz.qmd). Each exercise page ends with short, optional R tasks.

## From cells to an organism

A cell is surrounded by a selectively permeable membrane. The membrane helps
maintain differences between the cell and its surroundings. Transport proteins,
metabolic reactions and signalling processes contribute to those differences.
A multicellular animal adds extracellular fluid: most cells exchange with
nearby interstitial fluid rather than directly with the outside environment.
Blood, where present, transports materials between exchange organs and tissues.
This arrangement means the circulation, respiratory surface and cell membrane
are successive parts of one transport pathway.

A **tissue** combines cells and extracellular material in a functional
arrangement. An **organ** contains several tissue types. In the intestine,
an epithelial lining performs secretion and absorption, connective tissue
supports it, smooth muscle moves its contents, and nervous tissue coordinates
activity. An organ system groups interacting organs, but the boundaries of
systems are teaching conveniences: digestion depends on circulation, nervous
control and hormonal signals.

Draw an arrow from food in the gut to an absorbed nutrient in a muscle cell.
The nutrient must cross the gut epithelium, enter a transport route and cross
the muscle-cell membrane. Saying that digestion “gives the cells energy” skips
these steps and also skips metabolism. Digestion releases absorbable molecules;
cells subsequently transform chemical energy into ATP and other usable forms.

## Why geometry matters

Transport across a surface depends on how much surface is available and how
far material must move. To isolate the geometrical issue, imagine a cube with
side length $L$. Its surface area is $6L^2$ and its volume is $L^3$, so its
surface-area-to-volume ratio is $6/L$. The ratio has units of inverse length.
For a cube of side 1 mm it is 6 mm⁻¹; for a cube of side 2 mm it is 3 mm⁻¹.
Doubling length gives four times the surface but eight times the volume.

This does not mean that all large animals have low functional exchange areas.
It explains why their exchange surfaces cannot simply be smooth scaled-up
versions of a small body. Folding, branching and subdivision increase area;
thin barriers shorten diffusion paths; bulk flow transports material across
long distances. A mammal's lungs and circulation solve different parts of
the transport problem. Blood flow does not replace diffusion across the final
barrier between a capillary and a tissue cell.

Diffusion over a long distance is slow. In a simple comparison with the same
diffusing substance and conditions, the characteristic diffusion time grows
with the square of distance. Increasing distance tenfold therefore makes this
time scale roughly one hundredfold. This proportional argument explains the
value of thin exchange barriers without requiring an exact diffusion coefficient.
Real tissues also contain barriers, binding and flow, so the toy calculation
is a mechanism-building aid rather than a complete physiological prediction.

## Four tissue categories, many arrangements

For histology, start with what is visible and then make a functional inference.
**Epithelial tissue** forms sheets and boundaries. Cells are closely associated,
and one surface may face a lumen, meaning the inside space of a tube or cavity.
An epithelium has an apical side and a basal side; their transport proteins and
neighbours can differ. A thin single layer can support exchange, whereas several
layers can provide protection. Neither function follows from thickness alone:
location, junctions and specialised surfaces also matter.

**Connective tissue** contains cells within an extracellular matrix. The matrix
may be flexible, strong, mineralised or fluid. Tendon, cartilage, bone and blood
therefore differ substantially even though they belong to the same broad
category. A connective-tissue description should mention matrix organisation
rather than treating every pale space in a section as empty.

**Muscle tissue** develops force. Skeletal muscle typically has long striated
fibres with multiple nuclei. Cardiac muscle has striated branching cells and
specialised cell connections. Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped cells without
the same visible striation pattern. These are useful recognition clues, but
section angle and preparation affect appearance. **Nervous tissue** contains
neurons and supporting glial cells. Neurons receive, integrate and transmit
signals; glia contribute to the environment in which those signals operate.

In an actual section, record scale, orientation, cell shape, nuclear position,
layering, matrix and lumen relationships before proposing an identity. A circular
profile could be a cross-section of a tube rather than a spherical structure.
An organ name without supporting features is a guess. The descriptions used
in our exercises practise reasoning; they do not replace identifying the actual
course specimens. OpenStax provides openly accessible examples of the
[four primary tissue types](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/33-2-animal-primary-tissues).

## Regulated variables and negative feedback

An animal survives within ranges of temperature, fluid composition and other
conditions. **Homeostasis** is the active maintenance of suitable internal
conditions despite disturbances. It is dynamic: material and energy can enter
and leave while a measured variable remains approximately stable. Stability
does not mean that every organ is inactive or that every variable is constant.

A useful feedback explanation identifies a regulated variable, a disturbance,
a sensor, a control process, an effector and the consequence of the response.
For example, increased body temperature can be detected by thermosensory
systems. Neural control changes heat-loss or heat-production processes.
Those changes can oppose the original rise in temperature. In **negative
feedback**, the response reduces the deviation that helped trigger it.

The control process is not necessarily a single anatomical “control centre”,
and a target range can change with time or physiological state. Positive
feedback instead amplifies a change and needs some terminating condition.
It can be useful during a finite event, but it is not the standard explanation
for long-term stability. Feedback terminology refers to the direction of the
loop, not whether its consequences are desirable.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D[Disturbance raises body temperature] --> S[Temperature sensing]
  S --> C[Neural control]
  C --> E[Heat loss increases or heat production falls]
  E --> T[Body temperature moves towards defended range]
  T -->|Reduced deviation reduces response| S
```

This original functional sketch omits interacting pathways. Identify the
opposing effect of the response, rather than inferring feedback merely from
the diagram containing a loop.

Separate a controlled variable from an effector. In a thermal example, body
temperature may be the regulated variable, while skin blood flow is one
response that affects heat exchange. Observing increased blood flow does not
establish that blood flow itself was the variable defended by the system.
Use the [homeostasis reading](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/33-3-homeostasis)
to compare another feedback loop with this example.

## Comparison without a ladder of “better” animals

Different body plans face different constraints. A flat body can shorten
distances to the environment, but it also limits possible geometry. A hard
external covering can support and protect an animal while making exchange
through the whole body surface more difficult. An insect's tracheal system
delivers gases through branching air-filled tubes, whereas a mammal uses blood
for most oxygen delivery beyond the lung. These are alternative combinations
of mechanisms, not stages on a ladder towards a mammal.

Evolutionary **adaptation** concerns heritable features shaped across
generations. **Acclimation** concerns an individual's adjustment to changed
conditions, often under controlled conditions; acclimatisation is commonly
used for adjustment in a natural setting. A fish changing its physiological
performance after several weeks at a new temperature has not evolved during
that experiment. A short-term response, such as changing ventilation within
minutes, is also different from a sustained acclimatory change.

When explaining a trait, distinguish its current function from evidence about
its evolutionary origin. A structure being useful does not by itself prove
how it evolved. Comparisons are strongest when they connect environment,
mechanism, performance and relevant evidence, while allowing for trade-offs
and shared ancestry.
